paragraphs.heading: Switching viewpoints
paragraphs.text: The Lorentz transformations are the rules for converting coordinates from one frame in spacetime to another frame moving at a constant velocity relative to the first. They act on events, where an event is something that happens at one point in space at one instant, a single point in spacetime. The transformations link the space and time coordinates that observers in each frame give to the same event. They form a linear family with six parameters, named after the Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz.

paragraphs.heading: Replacing Galileo
paragraphs.text: They take the place of the Galilean transformation of Newton's physics, which assumes an absolute space and time. Galileo's version is a good approximation only when relative speeds are much lower than the speed of light. The Lorentz version has some unintuitive features: observers moving at different velocities can measure different distances, different elapsed times and even a different order of events. Through all of that, the speed of light stays the same in every inertial frame, which is one of the postulates of special relativity.

paragraphs.heading: The Lorentz factor
paragraphs.text: When the speed v is much smaller than c, the speed of light, the Lorentz factor γ is barely different from 1. As v gets closer to c, γ grows without bound, and v must stay below c for the transformation to give working solutions. Going back the other way uses the same transformation with the velocity's sign flipped.

paragraphs.heading: Only steady motion
paragraphs.text: Frames of reference come in two kinds: inertial ones, in relative motion at constant velocity, and non-inertial ones, which accelerate, follow curved paths or rotate. The name Lorentz transformation is used only for changes between inertial frames, usually in special relativity. In each frame an observer measures lengths with a local coordinate system, usually Cartesian, and time intervals with a clock.

paragraphs.heading: A geometric view
paragraphs.text: A Lorentz transformation can include a rotation of space; one with no rotation is called a Lorentz boost. In Minkowski space, the model of spacetime used in special relativity, these transformations keep the spacetime interval between any two events unchanged. They leave the event at the origin fixed and can be pictured as a hyperbolic rotation of Minkowski space. Adding translations as well gives a larger set known as the Poincaré group.

paragraphs.heading: From aether to Einstein
paragraphs.text: In the 1890s Lorentz was building theories of electrodynamics around an aether, and from 1892 to 1904 he used these transformations as mathematical aids. Woldemar Voigt had developed similar ones in 1887 while studying the Doppler shift. That same year a more accurate repeat of the Michelson–Morley experiment led George FitzGerald to suggest that bodies moving through the aether contract, an idea Lorentz presented independently and in more detail in 1892. In 1905 Henri Poincaré recognized that the transformations form a mathematical group and named it after Lorentz. That same year Albert Einstein derived them from the principle of relativity and the constant speed of light, setting the aether aside as unnecessary.
